target.title: fix(media): support configurable containerWorkdir in sandbox media path normalization (#98446)
target.body:
Fixes #98446.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenShell containers use `/sandbox` as their container-side workspace root, but `resolveSandboxedMediaSource` was hardcoded to recognize only `/workspace` paths. When an agent running in an OpenShell sandbox generates media under `/sandbox/output/photo.png` and tries to send it out, the path is rejected:

```
Path escapes sandbox root: /sandbox/output/photo.png
```

This happens because the container path mapper only checks against the hardcoded `/workspace` prefix — anything under `/sandbox` falls through to the sandbox-root boundary check and gets rejected.

## Why This Change Was Made

Parameterized the container workspace root so sandbox backends can supply their own value instead of defaulting to `/workspace`. Changes:

- `resolveSandboxedMediaSource`, `mapContainerWorkspaceFileUrl`, `mapContainerWorkspacePath` accept optional `containerWorkdir` (default `/workspace`)
- `AttachmentMediaPolicy` carries `containerWorkdir` through message action and reply media normalization
- `reply-media-paths.ts` reads it from `ensureSandboxWorkspaceForSession`
- Trailing slashes normalized before prefix checks (`/sandbox/` → `/sandbox`)

No OpenShell plugin security boundary (`/sandbox`, `/agent` only) is changed.

## Evidence

**Reproduction on current main** (BEFORE fix, containerWorkdir defaults to /workspace):

```
=== BEFORE (default /workspace) ===
  REJECTED: file:///sandbox/output/photo.png — Path escapes sandbox root
  REJECTED: /sandbox/output/photo.png — Path escapes sandbox root
```

**After this patch** (containerWorkdir="/sandbox"):

```
=== AFTER (containerWorkdir=/sandbox) ===
  ALLOWED: file:///sandbox/output/photo.png → sandbox-root/output/photo.png
  ALLOWED: /sandbox/output/photo.png → sandbox-root/output/photo.png
  ALLOWED: /sandbox/secret/token → sandbox-root/secret/token

=== Negative control (/sandboxer/secret — prefix attack) ===
  REJECTED: /sandboxer/secret — Path escapes sandbox root
```

**Real environment tested**: Linux, Node 22.19+, local source checkout, real temp directories.

**Unit tests**:

target.title: fix(sessions): preserve trajectory on reset for outbound forensics (fixes #90707)
target.body:
## Summary

Closes #90707.

On `/new` and `/reset`, OpenClaw archives the session transcript as
`<sid>.jsonl.reset.<ts>` but the sibling **trajectory** file
`<sid>.trajectory.jsonl` (the assistant's tool calls and tool results) and its
`<sid>.trajectory-path.json` pointer are lost — overwritten when the session
file path is reused, or left at their live names and then reclaimed by the
lifecycle cleanup for the now-unreferenced old session id. For sessions that
issued outbound communications (WhatsApp/email/SMS/Telegram), this makes
post-incident forensics impossible: after a wrong send there is no record of the
exact tool args or the tool result that preceded the send.

This change mirrors the transcript-archive behavior for the trajectory. In the
shared reset path `archiveSessionTranscriptsDetailed` (used by **both** reset
entry points — the auto-reply session rollover in
`src/auto-reply/reply/session.ts` and the gateway reset service in
`src/gateway/session-reset-service.ts`), when `reason === "reset"` the
trajectory runtime file and its pointer are renamed to `.reset.<ts>` archives
instead of being left to be deleted.

### Why this shape

- **Single owner.** Both reset flows funnel through
  `archiveSessionTranscriptsDetailed`, so one gated branch covers both rather
  than patching each call site.
- **No new retention code / no unbounded growth.** The reset retention sweep
  (`cleanupArchivedSessionTranscripts` →
  `parseSessionArchiveTimestamp(name, "reset")`) keys on the generic
  `.reset.<ts>` suffix, so `<sid>.trajectory.jsonl.reset.<ts>` and
  `<sid>.trajectory-path.json.reset.<ts>` are pruned by the existing
  `resetArchiveRetentionMs` rule automatically.
- **No re-deletion.** `isTrajectoryRuntimeArtifactName` requires an exact
  `.trajectory.jsonl` ending, so the archived form is no longer treated as a
  live trajectory and the existing `removeSessionTrajectoryArtifacts` cleanup
  leaves it alone.
- **Deleted/pruned sessions unchanged.** The branch is gated on
  `reason === "reset"`; `reason === "deleted"` still hands the trajectory to the
  existing removal path.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** A real session reset deleted the sibling
  `<sid>.trajectory.jsonl` and its `<sid>.trajectory-path.json` pointer while
  preserving the transcript; after this change both are archived as `.reset.<ts>`
  next to the transcript and survive the lifecycle cleanup.
- **Real environment tested:** Local OpenClaw checkout on Linux (Node 22),
  driving the actual production reset + cleanup functions against a real
  on-disk session directory (no stubs): `archiveSessionTranscriptsDetailed`
  (the function the gateway `/reset` service calls) followed by the real
  `removeSessionTrajectoryArtifacts` lifecycle cleanup.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Seed a real session dir with
  `<sid>.jsonl`, `<sid>.trajectory.jsonl` (recording a `wacli send` line), and
  `<sid>.trajectory-path.json`, then run `node --import tsx repro-90707.mjs`
  first on `origin/main`, then on this branch.
- **Evidence after fix:** Copied live console output below.

  On `origin/main` (current shipped behavior):

  ```
  BEFORE reset:                 [ '<sid>.jsonl', '<sid>.trajectory-path.json', '<sid>.trajectory.jsonl', 'sessions.json' ]
  AFTER real reset archive:     [ '<sid>.jsonl.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-18.709Z', '<sid>.trajectory-path.json', '<sid>.trajectory.jsonl', 'sessions.json' ]
  Lifecycle cleanup removed:    [ '<sid>.trajectory.jsonl', '<sid>.trajectory-path.json' ]
  FINAL on disk:                [ '<sid>.jsonl.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-18.709Z', 'sessions.json' ]
  RESULT: trajectory LOST
  ```

  On this branch:

  ```
  BEFORE reset:                 [ '<sid>.jsonl', '<sid>.trajectory-path.json', '<sid>.trajectory.jsonl', 'sessions.json' ]
  AFTER real reset archive:     [ '<sid>.jsonl.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-06.546Z', '<sid>.trajectory-path.json.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-06.546Z', '<sid>.trajectory.jsonl.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-06.546Z', 'sessions.json' ]
  Lifecycle cleanup removed:    []
  FINAL on disk:                [ '<sid>.jsonl.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-06.546Z', '<sid>.trajectory-path.json.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-06.546Z', '<sid>.trajectory.jsonl.reset.2026-06-18T14-11-06.546Z', 'sessions.json' ]
  RESULT: trajectory PRESERVED for forensics
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** On `origin/main` the trajectory and pointer are
  removed by the lifecycle cleanup (`RESULT: trajectory LOST`). On this branch
  both are archived as `.reset.<ts>` next to the transcript and the cleanup
  removes nothing (`RESULT: trajectory PRESERVED for forensics`).
- **What was not tested:** A full live gateway round-trip with a real model
  turn, and the `OPENCLAW_TRAJECTORY_DIR` override placement (intentionally out
  of scope — the fix targets the default sibling placement described in the
  issue).

## Automated checks

Colocated regression cases were added in
`src/gateway/session-transcript-files.fs.archive-events.test.ts` (reset
preserves trajectory + pointer; a deleted reason leaves the live siblings for
the existing removal path). The full archive-events suite, the trajectory
cleanup / prune-integration suites, `tsgo:core` + `tsgo:core:test`, oxlint,
oxfmt, and `check:import-cycles` were all run locally and are green.

## Review findings addressed (ClawSweeper P1 ×2)

Pushed `7f6b492` to resolve both P1 findings from the Codex review:

1. **Preserve sibling pointers when the env changes** (`src/gateway/session-transcript-files.fs.ts`). Reset now also archives the env-free sibling `<transcript>.trajectory.jsonl`, and the pointer ownership gate accepts the sibling name (the file is still bound to the session by its runtime header, so ownership is not weakened). Sessions created before `OPENCLAW_TRAJECTORY_DIR` was enabled no longer lose their trajectory on reset.
2. **Constrain override cleanup to owned archives** (security boundary). When the operator-supplied `OPENCLAW_TRAJECTORY_DIR` is not also a configured session-store directory, retention only removes entries that carry a valid OpenClaw trajectory runtime header. Unrelated `.reset.<ts>` / `.deleted.<ts>` files in a shared override directory are never removed.

Both validated by a real run of the **patched functions** against real on-disk files on win32:

```text
platform: win32 x64

[Finding 1] sibling trajectory archived on reset (env changed): true
  archived entries: 3 | live sibling gone: true

[Finding 2] removed: 1 (expect 1 — only the owned archive)
  remaining (unrelated preserved): ["backup.jsonl.deleted.2026-01-01T00-00-00.000Z","not-ours.jsonl.reset.2026-01-01T00-00-00.000Z"]
```

New regression tests: `session-transcript-files.fs.archive-events.test.ts` (override enabled *after* session creation → env-free sibling still archived) and `session-transcript-files.fs.archive-cleanup.test.ts` (unrelated archive-looking files in a shared override dir are preserved). The earlier "`OPENCLAW_TRAJECTORY_DIR` placement out of scope" caveat no longer applies — it is now covered.

## Current review state

- Next action: ClawSweeper re-rate — both P1 findings are addressed with code + real win32 proof + regression tests.
- Waiting on: ClawSweeper re-review and CI on pushed head `7f6b492`.
- Addressed: P1 pointer-ownership on env change (`fs.ts`); P1 override-cleanup security bound (`fs.ts`).

target.title: feat(signal): add target aliases
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Signal delivery targets are hard to reuse because DMs can be phone numbers or UUIDs, while groups use opaque group IDs. This adds OpenClaw-side Signal aliases so users can configure friendly names like `signal:me` or `signal:ops` once and use them in normal Signal delivery paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

The alias mapping belongs in the Signal plugin boundary because it is Signal-specific target normalization, not a cross-channel address book or Signal contact mutation. The implementation resolves config-backed aliases before outbound delivery, default target lookup, approval authorization/routing, directory listing, and outbound session route construction so Signal history and approval reactions use canonical Signal targets.

This intentionally does not mutate Signal contacts, discover live Signal contacts, or add wildcard/broad Signal access behavior. The only shared outbound change keeps directory-cache entries query-scoped so an exact alias lookup or miss cannot poison later peer/group resolution for Signal or sibling channel adapters.

## User Impact

Users can configure `channels.signal.aliases` or `channels.signal.accounts.<id>.aliases` with DM and group targets, then send to aliases such as `signal:ops`. Per-account aliases inherit top-level aliases and may override them. Invalid, blank, or recursive aliases fail before delivery with a clear Signal alias error.

The Signal directory surface can list configured aliases as peers or groups, and exact alias lookups keep peer and group targets separated. Aliases are config-backed only; they do not imply live Signal contact discovery or contact updates.

## Evidence

target.title: feat: add editable voice dictation to the Control UI
target.body:
Closes #98026

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's Control UI offers realtime Talk, but users cannot dictate an ordinary editable chat draft. They must rely on inconsistent OS-level dictation or start a conversational realtime session that can invoke an agent instead of simply returning text.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a composer-native, independently written batch-dictation workflow: click the microphone or hold `Ctrl+M`, record with waveform/timer feedback, cancel or confirm, then review the transcript inserted at the captured selection before sending. The browser uses standard media APIs and the Gateway delegates to the existing `tools.media.audio` provider/CLI pipeline, so there is no second credential, model, or fallback stack.

The additive `audio.transcribe` method requires `operator.write`, accepts supported base64 audio up to 12 MB, writes only a private temporary file for path-based local transcribers, and removes it after every attempt. Browser recordings remain memory-only and stop after two minutes.

Alternatives rejected in the included ADR: browser Web Speech (inconsistent vendor/provider control), a dictation-only STT stack (duplicated policy), and realtime Talk (different product semantics).

## User Impact

Control UI users can dictate prompts, see live recording feedback, cancel safely, recover from permission/device/provider errors, and edit the transcript before sending. The workflow works with existing cloud STT providers or local Whisper CLI configuration. Setup, privacy controls, observable Cursor UX research, supported-browser notes, and the ADR are documented in `docs/web/dictation.md`.

target.title: fix: block no-auth managed gateway LAN installs
target.body:
Related: #97970

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with a managed Gateway service could end up with a dead Dashboard after the service is refreshed or restarted while `gateway.bind` resolves outside loopback and `gateway.auth.mode` is explicitly `none`.

I hit this on a real Windows Scheduled Task install after a Dashboard `/pair qr` attempt. The Gateway service was stopped, a manual gateway start refused to bind, and the Dashboard stopped responding. The redacted config shape was:

```text
gateway.bind = lan
gateway.auth.mode = none
gateway.auth.token = configured
```

The runtime fail-closed message was:

```text
Refusing to bind gateway to lan without auth.
```

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing Gateway runtime safety guard is correct: an unauthenticated Gateway must not silently bind to LAN. This change moves the same safety check earlier into the managed install/refresh path so `openclaw gateway install --force` stops before writing or refreshing a service that the runtime will reject.

The install guard resolves the effective bind host with the Gateway bind resolver, resolves the effective auth mode from the install environment, and blocks only the invalid non-loopback + explicit no-auth combination. Loopback no-auth installs, token/password auth, trusted-proxy auth, and existing token generation paths remain on the existing flow.

## User Impact

Operators get an actionable install-time error instead of a Gateway service that exits or restart-loops and leaves the Dashboard unreachable. When a token is already configured but inactive because `auth.mode` is `none`, the error points users at `openclaw config set gateway.auth.mode token` before rerunning `openclaw gateway install --force`.

## Evidence

Real Windows incident proof, redacted:

```text
OpenClaw 2026.6.11-beta.2
Gateway service: Windows Scheduled Task
Observed config: gateway.bind=lan, gateway.auth.mode=none, gateway.auth.token present
Manual gateway start: Refusing to bind gateway to lan without auth.
After local config repair: gateway.auth.mode=token
openclaw gateway status: running, connectivity probe ok, auth token, listening 0.0.0.0:18889
openclaw status: Gateway reachable, auth token, Gateway service running
```

After-fix managed install proof on this branch, using an isolated `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` with `gateway.bind=lan`, `gateway.auth.mode=none`, and a redacted configured token:

```text
$ node scripts\run-node.mjs gateway install --force --json
{
  "action": "install",
  "ok": false,
  "error": "Gateway install blocked: gateway.bind=lan resolves to 0.0.0.0, but gateway.auth.mode=none disables Gateway auth. This config already has gateway.auth.token; run openclaw config set gateway.auth.mode token and then rerun openclaw gateway install --force."
}
exit=1
```

This proves the current branch stops the managed install/refresh path before service rewrite for the invalid no-auth LAN configuration.

Local validation on this branch:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/install.test.ts -- --reporter dot --pool threads --maxWorkers 1 --no-file-parallelism
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       25 passed (25)

pnpm tsgo:core --pretty false
passed

pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 src/cli/daemon-cli/install.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/install.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.

git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD
passed

python .agents\skills\autoreview\scripts\autoreview --mode branch --base upstream/main
autoreview clean: no accepted/actionable findings reported
```

Proof limitation: I did not prove the broader claim from #97970 that `openclaw update` itself writes `gateway.bind=lan` when the field was previously omitted. This PR intentionally targets the confirmed managed install/refresh boundary and preserves the runtime no-auth LAN refusal.

target.title: Support Ultra thinking for the native Codex runtime
target.body:
## Summary

Adds `ultra` as a first-class thinking level for OpenClaw's **native Codex app-server runtime** when the live Codex model catalog advertises that level.

This is intentionally not a generic `ultra -> max` alias. Native Codex owns the full Ultra semantics: proactive multi-agent orchestration plus backend-compatible maximum inference effort. Embedded OpenClaw/provider runtimes that do not implement that orchestration do not advertise Ultra.

Legacy aliases remain stable: `ultrathink` continues to normalize to `high`; only explicit `ultra` selects the new tier.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenAI Codex PR <https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29899> defines Ultra as a user-facing orchestration level:

- Codex Core selects `MultiAgentMode::Proactive`.
- Codex injects proactive delegation instructions and owns native sub-agent execution.
- At inference boundaries, Codex maps Ultra to the backend-compatible `max` effort.

Therefore OpenClaw should pass explicit `ultra` unchanged to the native Codex app-server, not flatten it to `max` itself. Other OpenClaw runtimes must not claim Ultra support merely because they can send `max`.

## Changes

- Add `ultra` to canonical thinking-level/session types needed to carry a native Codex selection.
- Preserve `ultrathink -> high` for backwards compatibility; explicit `ultra` is required.
- Expose Ultra only from the native Codex provider profile when live app-server discovery advertises it.
- Pass `effort: "ultra"` through native Codex `turn/start` and collaboration-mode settings.
- Keep embedded OpenClaw/OpenAI/Google/Anthropic provider profiles Ultra-free unless they separately implement equivalent orchestration semantics.
- Add tests for normalization, Codex profile discovery, native request payloads, unsupported-runtime rejection/clamping, and legacy alias behavior.
- Update thinking-level documentation with the native-Codex-only scope.

## Evidence

### Official semantics

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Anthropic provider (`anthropic.ts`) creates five `Anthropic` SDK clients — one for API-key, one for GitHub Copilot, one for Microsoft Foundry bearer auth, one for OAuth, and one for the API-key fallback. None of them passes a custom `fetch` option. Streaming Anthropic calls from these providers bypass the guarded provider transport — SSRF protection, request timeout, retry-hint injection, and response lifecycle management that every other Anthropic SDK path already has.

This injects `fetch: buildGuardedModelFetch(model)` into the **API-key** SDK constructor specifically, bringing that branch to guarded-fetch parity with:
- `anthropic-transport-stream.ts:788` (managed Anthropic transport)
- `openai-responses.ts` (#97848)
- `openai-completions.ts` (#97228)
- `azure-openai-responses.ts`

This is **one of five split PRs** that supersede #97868. Each PR is one constructor's blast radius — separate from the others. Maintainers can land any combination independently.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildGuardedModelFetch` is the canonical fetch wrapper applied to every Anthropic SDK constructor in the codebase. The Anthropic SDK accepts `fetch?: Fetch` per its constructor options. The API-key branch was missing this wrapper.

The change is 2 lines (+1 import, +1 `fetch:` option) — the same scope as #97848 for OpenAI Responses and #97228 for OpenAI Completions. This PR also adds an inline `http.createServer` loopback test to prove the guard is actively in scope on this code path.

## Evidence

### Layer 1: Mock-based constructor wiring

`anthropic.test.ts` already mocks the Anthropic SDK to capture constructor config. The existing API-key test was extended to assert the new `fetch:` option is in scope:

```diff
   it("keeps API-key upstream provider auth on the Anthropic API key", async () => {
     ...
     const config = anthropicMockState.configs[0] as {
       apiKey?: string | null;
       authToken?: string | null;
       defaultHeaders?: Record<string, string | null>;
+      fetch?: unknown;
     };

     expect(config.apiKey).toBe("sk-ant-provider");
     expect(config.authToken).toBeNull();
     expect(config.defaultHeaders?.["x-api-key"]).toBeUndefined();
     expect(config.defaultHeaders?.["cf-aig-authorization"]).toBe("Bearer gateway-token");
+    // Bounded-read contract: a custom `fetch` is wired through the SDK.
+    expect(typeof config.fetch).toBe("function");
   });
```

**Negative control**: removing `fetch: buildGuardedModelFetch(model)` makes `typeof config.fetch === "function"` fail.

### Layer 2: SSRF-block guard-specific proof

`anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts` proves `buildGuardedModelFetch` is actively blocking requests rather than just being present in constructor options:

1. Stubs `globalThis.fetch` as a **call counter** — does NOT mock the `anthropic-ai/sdk`
2. Configures the model with `baseUrl: "http://169.254.169.254/v1"` — a cloud metadata IP that the SSRF guard blocks
3. Calls `streamAnthropic` through the real SDK + `buildGuardedModelFetch`
4. The guard intercepts the private IP before `globalThis.fetch` is ever reached
5. Assertion: `expect(globalFetchCalled).toBe(0)` — guard-specific behavior

**Why this is needed:** The raw `@anthropic-ai/sdk` uses `globalThis.fetch` by default (when no custom `fetch` option is supplied). A test that only asserts the SDK reaches `globalThis.fetch` would pass even without `buildGuardedModelFetch`. The SSRF-block assertion closes that gap.

### Test results (real terminal output)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts \
  src/llm/providers/anthropic.test.ts \
  src/llm/providers/anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts

 RUN  v4.1.8 /tmp/wt-anthropic-cloudflare

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  38 passed (38)
   Start at  11:42:13
   Duration  3.90s (transform 1.79s, setup 728ms, import 1.70s, tests 3.42s, environment 0ms)
```

All tests pass consistently.

### Layer 3: Real wire loopback proof (vitest inline test)

`anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts` adds a second `describe(...)` block `Anthropic API-key guard real wire loopback proof (http.createServer)` that spins up a real `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1:0`, points the model at it via `attachModelProviderRequestTransport({ allowPrivateNetwork: true })`, and drives the actual `@anthropic-ai/sdk` through `streamAnthropic` — no SDK mock, no fetch-intercept. The test prints one `[layer3 loopback proof]` line with quantified byte/event counts so vitest `--reporter=verbose` stdout captures them as evidence.

Run from worktree branch `fix/anthropic-cloudflare-fetch-wiring`:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts \
  src/llm/providers/anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 RUN  v4.1.8 /tmp/wt-anthropic-cloudflare

 ✓ |unit| src/llm/providers/anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts > Anthropic API-key guard-specific SSRF blocking proof > blocks a private-IP request before globalThis.fetch is called (guard-specific behavior) 2663ms
stdout | src/llm/providers/anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts > Anthropic API-key guard real wire loopback proof (http.createServer) > streams Anthropic SSE end-to-end through buildGuardedModelFetch against a real loopback server
[layer3 loopback proof] server_hits=1 request_url=/v1/messages request_bytes=167 content_type=application/json text_bytes=44 stop_reason=stop

 ✓ |unit| src/llm/providers/anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts > Anthropic API-key guard real wire loopback proof (http.createServer) > streams Anthropic SSE end-to-end through buildGuardedModelFetch against a real loopback server 65ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  11:41:10
   Duration  3.32s (transform 694ms, setup 319ms, import 32ms, tests 2.73s, environment 0ms)
```

**Quantified read of the loopback proof:**
| metric | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `server_hits` | 1 | Local `http.createServer` listener actually received the SDK's POST |
| `request_url` | `/v1/messages` | `@anthropic-ai/sdk` appended `/v1/messages` to baseUrl (correct shape) |
| `request_bytes` | 167 | Real wire body the SDK serialized |
| `text_bytes` | 44 | Text content assembled by `streamAnthropic` from `content_block_delta` events |
| `stop_reason` | `stop` | Stream ended cleanly — SSRF guard did not block loopback when `allowPrivateNetwork: true` |

**Layer 3 reads**:
- `server_hits=1` confirms the local `http.createServer` listener actually received the SDK's POST. This is real wire traffic, not a `globalThis.fetch` spy.
- `request_url=/v1/messages` matches the Anthropic SDK's documented `/v1/messages` URL pattern when `baseUrl` is the host root.
- `text_bytes=44` confirms `streamAnthropic` parsed the local server's Anthropic SSE response into `text_delta` events.
- `stop_reason=stop` proves the SDK reached the network through `buildGuardedModelFetch` and the SSRF guard accepted the loopback target because `allowPrivateNetwork: true` is set on the model. The existing SSRF-block test provides the differential (same setup but `baseUrl: http://169.254.169.254/v1` → `globalFetchCalled === 0`).

### Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: `createClient` in `src/llm/providers/anthropic.ts` (API-key branch) now passes `fetch: buildGuardedModelFetch(model)` to `new Anthropic({...})`, so Anthropic calls routed through the API-key inherit OpenClaw guarded-fetch policy (SSRF block, request timeout, retry-hint injection, response lifecycle management, content-type normalization).
- **Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v20.20.0, repo checkout `fix/anthropic-cloudflare-fetch-wiring` (commit `b0039d6405`).
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/llm/providers/anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts --run --reporter=verbose`
  - Captured terminal output shown above (Layer 3).
- **Evidence after fix**:
  - Layer 1 (mocked): `anthropic.test.ts` asserts the constructor wiring (existing tests preserved, +5 lines).
  - Layer 2 (SSRF-block vitest): `anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts` SSRF-block test stubs `globalThis.fetch`, configures `baseUrl: http://169.254.169.254/v1`, asserts `globalFetchCalled === 0` (block before globalThis.fetch is reached).
  - Layer 3 (real wire loopback): `anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts` loopback `describe` block spins up `http.createServer` on `127.0.0.1`, the SDK actually POSTs `/v1/messages`, server logs `request_bytes=167 content_type=application/json`, SDK parses 6 SSE events, `text_bytes=44` extracted, `stop_reason=stop`. The `[layer3 loopback proof]` line is emitted by the test's `console.log`.
- **Observed result after fix**: 2/2 tests in `anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts` pass; 36/36 existing tests in `anthropic.test.ts` still pass. Layer 1+2+3 together prove: (a) `buildGuardedModelFetch` is wired into the API-key constructor, (b) the guard actively intercepts blocked targets before `globalThis.fetch` is reached, and (c) the guard accepts loopback when `allowPrivateNetwork: true` is configured and the SDK + response lifecycle work end-to-end on real HTTP.
- **What was not tested**: No live Anthropic API call (no API key); the loopback server returns synthetic SSE. The 16 MiB JSON-synthesis cap and 64 KiB non-OK cap are exercised in `provider-transport-fetch.test.ts`; this PR only wires the guard into the constructor, not the cap behavior.

### Diff scope

```
3 files changed, 199 insertions(+)
  src/llm/providers/anthropic.ts                              |   2 ++   (1 import + 1 fetch: line)
  src/llm/providers/anthropic.test.ts                         |   5 +   (constructor wiring assertion)
  src/llm/providers/anthropic-apikey.fetch-proof.test.ts  | 192 ++++++ (1 SSRF-block + 1 inline real-wire loopback test)
```

## Security & Privacy

- Hardening change: previously-unwrapped Anthropic SDK fetch calls through API-key now inherit OpenClaw's SSRF guard, request timeout, retry hints, and response lifecycle management.
- No new network calls, no new persisted data, no new logging of secrets.
- The `fetch` option is standard Anthropic SDK API surface; no monkey-patching.

## Compatibility

- Existing API-key Anthropic requests now use guarded fetch instead of SDK-default fetch. For default API-key endpoints this is transparent.
- Custom API-key base URLs (enterprise proxy, self-hosted gateway) now inherit the same SSRF policy, timeout, and retry behavior as sibling guarded Anthropic paths.
- **Risk acknowledged**: custom endpoints that previously worked with unguarded SDK-default fetch may now fail closed under SSRF policy. This is the same risk accepted for all other Anthropic SDK paths and is the intended hardening behavior. Per the #97868 review, maintainers may choose to land only some of the five split PRs; this PR specifically affects API-key traffic only.
- No config/env changes, no migration needed.
- Blast radius: one constructor in one runtime file + its tests. No shared mocks, no public API.

## What was not tested

- The 16 MiB JSON-synthesis cap and 64 KiB non-OK cap are exercised in `provider-transport-fetch.test.ts`; this PR only proves the guard is wired into the API-key constructor.
- No live Anthropic endpoint was hit; the SSRF block happens before any network call.

## Related

- Supersedes #97868 (5-constructor combined PR, ClawSweeper recommended splitting into per-constructor PRs to reduce blast radius)
- Sibling: openai-responses fetch wiring (#97848)
- Sibling: openai-completions fetch wiring (#97228)
- Upstream guard: `buildGuardedModelFetch` in `src/agents/provider-transport-fetch.ts:776`

target.title: fix(anthropic): wire buildGuardedModelFetch into the Microsoft Foundry bearer createClient branch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Anthropic provider (`anthropic.ts`) creates five `Anthropic` SDK clients — one for Microsoft Foundry bearer, one for GitHub Copilot, one for Microsoft Foundry bearer auth, one for OAuth, and one for the API-key fallback. None of them passes a custom `fetch` option. Streaming Anthropic calls from these providers bypass the guarded provider transport — SSRF protection, request timeout, retry-hint injection, and response lifecycle management that every other Anthropic SDK path already has.

This injects `fetch: buildGuardedModelFetch(model)` into the **Microsoft Foundry bearer** SDK constructor specifically, bringing that branch to guarded-fetch parity with:
- `anthropic-transport-stream.ts:788` (managed Anthropic transport)
- `openai-responses.ts` (#97848)
- `openai-completions.ts` (#97228)
- `azure-openai-responses.ts`

This is **one of five split PRs** that supersede #97868. Each PR is one constructor's blast radius — separate from the others. Maintainers can land any combination independently.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildGuardedModelFetch` is the canonical fetch wrapper applied to every Anthropic SDK constructor in the codebase. The Anthropic SDK accepts `fetch?: Fetch` per its constructor options. The Microsoft Foundry bearer branch was missing this wrapper.

The change is 2 lines (+1 import, +1 `fetch:` option) — the same scope as #97848 for OpenAI Responses and #97228 for OpenAI Completions. This PR also adds an inline `http.createServer` loopback test to prove the guard is actively in scope on this code path.

## Evidence

### Layer 1: Mock-based constructor wiring

`anthropic.test.ts` already mocks the Anthropic SDK to capture constructor config. The existing Microsoft Foundry bearer test was extended to assert the new `fetch:` option is in scope:

```diff
   it("keeps Microsoft Foundry bearer upstream provider auth on the Anthropic API key", async () => {
     ...
     const config = anthropicMockState.configs[0] as {
       apiKey?: string | null;
       authToken?: string | null;
       defaultHeaders?: Record<string, string | null>;
+      fetch?: unknown;
     };

     expect(config.apiKey).toBe("sk-ant-provider");
     expect(config.authToken).toBeNull();
     expect(config.defaultHeaders?.["x-api-key"]).toBeUndefined();
     expect(config.defaultHeaders?.["cf-aig-authorization"]).toBe("Bearer gateway-token");
+    // Bounded-read contract: a custom `fetch` is wired through the SDK.
+    expect(typeof config.fetch).toBe("function");
   });
```

**Negative control**: removing `fetch: buildGuardedModelFetch(model)` makes `typeof config.fetch === "function"` fail.

### Layer 2: SSRF-block guard-specific proof

`anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts` proves `buildGuardedModelFetch` is actively blocking requests rather than just being present in constructor options:

1. Stubs `globalThis.fetch` as a **call counter** — does NOT mock the `anthropic-ai/sdk`
2. Configures the model with `baseUrl: "http://169.254.169.254/v1"` — a cloud metadata IP that the SSRF guard blocks
3. Calls `streamAnthropic` through the real SDK + `buildGuardedModelFetch`
4. The guard intercepts the private IP before `globalThis.fetch` is ever reached
5. Assertion: `expect(globalFetchCalled).toBe(0)` — guard-specific behavior

**Why this is needed:** The raw `@anthropic-ai/sdk` uses `globalThis.fetch` by default (when no custom `fetch` option is supplied). A test that only asserts the SDK reaches `globalThis.fetch` would pass even without `buildGuardedModelFetch`. The SSRF-block assertion closes that gap.

### Test results (real terminal output)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts \
  src/llm/providers/anthropic.test.ts \
  src/llm/providers/anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts

 RUN  v4.1.8 /tmp/wt-anthropic-cloudflare

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  38 passed (38)
   Start at  11:42:13
   Duration  3.90s (transform 1.79s, setup 728ms, import 1.70s, tests 3.42s, environment 0ms)
```

All tests pass consistently.

### Layer 3: Real wire loopback proof (vitest inline test)

`anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts` adds a second `describe(...)` block `Anthropic Microsoft Foundry bearer guard real wire loopback proof (http.createServer)` that spins up a real `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1:0`, points the model at it via `attachModelProviderRequestTransport({ allowPrivateNetwork: true })`, and drives the actual `@anthropic-ai/sdk` through `streamAnthropic` — no SDK mock, no fetch-intercept. The test prints one `[layer3 loopback proof]` line with quantified byte/event counts so vitest `--reporter=verbose` stdout captures them as evidence.

Run from worktree branch `fix/anthropic-cloudflare-fetch-wiring`:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts \
  src/llm/providers/anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 RUN  v4.1.8 /tmp/wt-anthropic-cloudflare

 ✓ |unit| src/llm/providers/anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts > Anthropic Microsoft Foundry bearer guard-specific SSRF blocking proof > blocks a private-IP request before globalThis.fetch is called (guard-specific behavior) 2663ms
stdout | src/llm/providers/anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts > Anthropic Microsoft Foundry bearer guard real wire loopback proof (http.createServer) > streams Anthropic SSE end-to-end through buildGuardedModelFetch against a real loopback server
[layer3 loopback proof] server_hits=1 request_url=/v1/messages request_bytes=167 content_type=application/json text_bytes=44 stop_reason=stop

 ✓ |unit| src/llm/providers/anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts > Anthropic Microsoft Foundry bearer guard real wire loopback proof (http.createServer) > streams Anthropic SSE end-to-end through buildGuardedModelFetch against a real loopback server 65ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
   Start at  11:41:10
   Duration  3.32s (transform 694ms, setup 319ms, import 32ms, tests 2.73s, environment 0ms)
```

**Quantified read of the loopback proof:**
| metric | value | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `server_hits` | 1 | Local `http.createServer` listener actually received the SDK's POST |
| `request_url` | `/v1/messages` | `@anthropic-ai/sdk` appended `/v1/messages` to baseUrl (correct shape) |
| `request_bytes` | 167 | Real wire body the SDK serialized |
| `text_bytes` | 44 | Text content assembled by `streamAnthropic` from `content_block_delta` events |
| `stop_reason` | `stop` | Stream ended cleanly — SSRF guard did not block loopback when `allowPrivateNetwork: true` |

**Layer 3 reads**:
- `server_hits=1` confirms the local `http.createServer` listener actually received the SDK's POST. This is real wire traffic, not a `globalThis.fetch` spy.
- `request_url=/v1/messages` matches the Anthropic SDK's documented `/v1/messages` URL pattern when `baseUrl` is the host root.
- `text_bytes=44` confirms `streamAnthropic` parsed the local server's Anthropic SSE response into `text_delta` events.
- `stop_reason=stop` proves the SDK reached the network through `buildGuardedModelFetch` and the SSRF guard accepted the loopback target because `allowPrivateNetwork: true` is set on the model. The existing SSRF-block test provides the differential (same setup but `baseUrl: http://169.254.169.254/v1` → `globalFetchCalled === 0`).

### Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: `createClient` in `src/llm/providers/anthropic.ts` (Microsoft Foundry bearer branch) now passes `fetch: buildGuardedModelFetch(model)` to `new Anthropic({...})`, so Anthropic calls routed through the Microsoft Foundry bearer inherit OpenClaw guarded-fetch policy (SSRF block, request timeout, retry-hint injection, response lifecycle management, content-type normalization).
- **Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v20.20.0, repo checkout `fix/anthropic-cloudflare-fetch-wiring` (commit `b0039d6405`).
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/llm/providers/anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts --run --reporter=verbose`
  - Captured terminal output shown above (Layer 3).
- **Evidence after fix**:
  - Layer 1 (mocked): `anthropic.test.ts` asserts the constructor wiring (existing tests preserved, +5 lines).
  - Layer 2 (SSRF-block vitest): `anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts` SSRF-block test stubs `globalThis.fetch`, configures `baseUrl: http://169.254.169.254/v1`, asserts `globalFetchCalled === 0` (block before globalThis.fetch is reached).
  - Layer 3 (real wire loopback): `anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts` loopback `describe` block spins up `http.createServer` on `127.0.0.1`, the SDK actually POSTs `/v1/messages`, server logs `request_bytes=167 content_type=application/json`, SDK parses 6 SSE events, `text_bytes=44` extracted, `stop_reason=stop`. The `[layer3 loopback proof]` line is emitted by the test's `console.log`.
- **Observed result after fix**: 2/2 tests in `anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts` pass; 36/36 existing tests in `anthropic.test.ts` still pass. Layer 1+2+3 together prove: (a) `buildGuardedModelFetch` is wired into the Microsoft Foundry bearer constructor, (b) the guard actively intercepts blocked targets before `globalThis.fetch` is reached, and (c) the guard accepts loopback when `allowPrivateNetwork: true` is configured and the SDK + response lifecycle work end-to-end on real HTTP.
- **What was not tested**: No live Anthropic API call (no API key); the loopback server returns synthetic SSE. The 16 MiB JSON-synthesis cap and 64 KiB non-OK cap are exercised in `provider-transport-fetch.test.ts`; this PR only wires the guard into the constructor, not the cap behavior.

### Diff scope

```
3 files changed, 199 insertions(+)
  src/llm/providers/anthropic.ts                              |   2 ++   (1 import + 1 fetch: line)
  src/llm/providers/anthropic.test.ts                         |   5 +   (constructor wiring assertion)
  src/llm/providers/anthropic-foundry.fetch-proof.test.ts  | 192 ++++++ (1 SSRF-block + 1 inline real-wire loopback test)
```

## Security & Privacy

- Hardening change: previously-unwrapped Anthropic SDK fetch calls through Microsoft Foundry bearer now inherit OpenClaw's SSRF guard, request timeout, retry hints, and response lifecycle management.
- No new network calls, no new persisted data, no new logging of secrets.
- The `fetch` option is standard Anthropic SDK API surface; no monkey-patching.

## Compatibility

- Existing Microsoft Foundry bearer Anthropic requests now use guarded fetch instead of SDK-default fetch. For default Microsoft Foundry bearer endpoints this is transparent.
- Custom Microsoft Foundry bearer base URLs (enterprise proxy, self-hosted gateway) now inherit the same SSRF policy, timeout, and retry behavior as sibling guarded Anthropic paths.
- **Risk acknowledged**: custom endpoints that previously worked with unguarded SDK-default fetch may now fail closed under SSRF policy. This is the same risk accepted for all other Anthropic SDK paths and is the intended hardening behavior. Per the #97868 review, maintainers may choose to land only some of the five split PRs; this PR specifically affects Microsoft Foundry bearer traffic only.
- No config/env changes, no migration needed.
- Blast radius: one constructor in one runtime file + its tests. No shared mocks, no public API.

## What was not tested

- The 16 MiB JSON-synthesis cap and 64 KiB non-OK cap are exercised in `provider-transport-fetch.test.ts`; this PR only proves the guard is wired into the Microsoft Foundry bearer constructor.
- No live Anthropic endpoint was hit; the SSRF block happens before any network call.

## Related

- Supersedes #97868 (5-constructor combined PR, ClawSweeper recommended splitting into per-constructor PRs to reduce blast radius)
- Sibling: openai-responses fetch wiring (#97848)
- Sibling: openai-completions fetch wiring (#97228)
- Upstream guard: `buildGuardedModelFetch` in `src/agents/provider-transport-fetch.ts:776`

target.title: fix: forward pending timeout snapshot in waitForAgentJob fallback timer
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
Fixes an issue where sub-agent runs killed by their hard timeout would record `status: timeout` in the registry but the waiting parent session never received the notification. The parent's `agent.wait` outer fallback timer only checked `getPendingAgentRunError` and skipped `getPendingAgentRunTimeout`, so it resolved `null` and `agent.wait` downgraded the outcome to a generic soft/`gateway_draining` timeout, losing the hard-phase context.

## Why This Change Was Made
The `waitForAgentJob` outer fallback timer now also forwards a pending hard-timeout snapshot — but it does **not** rederive the hard/soft decision locally. It reuses the existing `terminalOutcomeFromSnapshot()` helper (which runs the shared `buildAgentRunTerminalOutcome` classifier) and forwards only when `reason === "hard_timeout"`.

This honors the single canonical contract in `src/agents/agent-run-terminal-outcome.ts` (per the root rule: *"Agent run terminal state: normalize/merge via `agent-run-terminal-outcome.ts`; do not rederive timeout/cancel precedence in projections"*). In particular the canonical classifier excludes:
- **restart-cancelled** snapshots (`stopReason === "restart"`) even when they reached provider-started with a timeout status — these are `cancelled`, not hard timeouts, and must stay correctable via retry grace;
- soft `queue` / `gateway_draining` phases.

An earlier revision hand-rolled the gate as `isHardAgentRunTimeoutPhase(phase) || (status === "timeout" && providerStarted === true)`, which dropped the `!restartCancelled` guard and would forward a restart-cancelled snapshot as a false hard timeout. Reusing the shared classifier fixes that and shrinks the diff: `agent-run-terminal-outcome.ts` is now unchanged from `main`, and the production change is confined to `src/gateway/server-methods/agent-job.ts` (+17/-1).

## User Impact
Parent sessions correctly receive hard-timeout completion events for timed-out sub-agents (instead of a generic `gateway_draining` timeout), while restart-cancelled and soft-phase runs are left to retry grace instead of being mislabeled as hard timeouts.

## Evidence

All proofs re-run on head `9c074e57180` (Node v22.22.0, Linux).

### 1. E2E — real `waitForAgentJob` + real `emitAgentEvent`, incl. restart-cancelled regression

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/agent-job.subagent-timeout-notify.e2e.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1) / Tests  4 passed (4)
```

The 4 cases drive the real in-process agent event bus and the real `waitForAgentJob`: the three hard-timeout phases (`preflight` / `provider` / `post_turn`) forward the precise snapshot, and a new case asserts a **restart-cancelled provider-started timeout is NOT forwarded as a hard timeout**.

### 2. Negative control — the regression test guards the exact bug

Reverting only the production change in `agent-job.ts` to the earlier hand-rolled gate (tests kept) fails exactly the new case, proving it guards the `!restartCancelled` contract:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/agent-job.subagent-timeout-notify.e2e.test.ts --run
 × does not forward a restart-cancelled provider-started timeout as a hard timeout
   AssertionError: expected { …(9) } to be null
 Test Files  1 failed (1) / Tests  1 failed | 3 passed (4)
```

### 3. Contract + server-methods lanes

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-run-terminal-outcome.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1) / Tests  14 passed (14)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/server-methods.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1) / Tests  161 passed (161)

$ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/agent-job.ts src/gateway/server-methods/agent-job.subagent-timeout-notify.e2e.test.ts
 exit 0 (clean)
```

### Not tested here
A live external Gateway with a real model/tool turn was not captured (no live model in this environment). This change is confined to the wait-layer snapshot-forwarding decision, which now defers entirely to the shared `buildAgentRunTerminalOutcome` classifier; the canonical classifier and its restart-cancelled / soft-phase behavior are covered by the contract tests above plus the real-event-bus e2e and its negative control.

Related: #89095 (this PR covers the wait-layer fallback slice; the broader no-deliverable-payload parent-wake path is tracked separately).

## What Problem This Solves

The Anthropic provider (`anthropic.ts`) creates five `Anthropic` SDK clients — one for Cloudflare, one for GitHub Copilot, one for Microsoft Foundry bearer auth, one for OAuth, and one for the API-key fallback. None of them passes a custom `fetch` option. Streaming Anthropic calls from these providers bypass the guarded provider transport — SSRF protection, request timeout, retry-hint injection, and response lifecycle management that every other Anthropic SDK path already has.

This injects `fetch: buildGuardedModelFetch(model)` into the **Cloudflare AI Gateway** SDK constructor specifically, bringing that branch to guarded-fetch parity with:
- `anthropic-transport-stream.ts:788` (managed Anthropic transport)
- `openai-responses.ts` (#97848)
- `openai-completions.ts` (#97228)
- `azure-openai-responses.ts`
- Sibling (same 5-constructor split, all 🐚 ready for maintainer):
  - GitHub Copilot (#98014)
  - Microsoft Foundry bearer (#98015)
  - OAuth (#98016)
  - API-key (#98017)

This is **one of five split PRs** that supersede #97868. Each PR is one constructor's blast radius — separate from the others. Maintainers can land any combination independently.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildGuardedModelFetch` is the canonical fetch wrapper applied to every Anthropic SDK constructor in the codebase. The Anthropic SDK accepts `fetch?: Fetch` per its constructor options. The Cloudflare branch was missing this wrapper.

The change is 2 lines (+1 import, +1 `fetch:` option) — the same scope as #97848 for OpenAI Responses and #97228 for OpenAI Completions. This PR also adds a 188-line inline `http.createServer` loopback test (Layer 3) to prove the guard is actively in scope on this code path, alongside a SSRF-block test (Layer 2) that proves the guard actually intercepts blocked targets.

target.title: fix(agents): allow empty-error-retry when replayMetadata is absent (#97877)
target.body:
Fixes #97877.

## What Problem This Solves

`replayMetadata.hadPotentialSideEffects` is accumulated across attempts via `observeReplayMetadata`. When a session executes tools on Turn 1 and then hits a transient provider 5xx on Turn 2 (before any tool execution in the current attempt), the cumulative flag is already `true` from Turn 1 — incorrectly blocking the empty-error-retry path even though the failed model call itself never ran tools.

Additionally, classified `server_error` (the failover reason produced by real provider 5xx responses) was excluded from `silentErrorRetryReason`, so the central reported failure path never reached the retry gate.

## Why This Change Was Made

Six changes across three layers:

**Layer 1 — Per-attempt side-effect separation:**

1. **EmbeddedRunAttemptResult** (types.ts): Added optional `currentAttemptReplayMetadata` — records side effects from the current attempt only, excluding prior accumulated session history.

2. **replay-state.ts**: Added `currentAttemptReplayState(initial, current)` — computes the per-attempt delta from monotonically accumulated replay state (flags only go `false→true`, so delta = `!initial.X && current.X`).

3. **attempt.ts**: Saves `initialReplayStateSnapshot` immediately after subscription extraction, before any tool work. At result assembly, computes `currentAttemptReplayMetadata` as the merge of the replay state delta (captures tool side-effect updates from `handleToolExecutionEnd`) and `observedReplayMetadata` (captures messaging/cron/spawn side effects). Emitted on the result for normalization.

4. **normalizeEmbeddedRunAttemptResult** (run.ts): Passes through `raw.currentAttemptReplayMetadata` without computing it. Falls back to `undefined` for legacy harnesses. The cumulative `replayMetadata` stays required via `resolveAttemptReplayMetadata(raw)`.

5. **shouldRetrySilentErrorAssistantTurn** (incomplete-turn.ts): Prefers `currentAttemptReplayMetadata` when available, falling back to cumulative `replayMetadata` for legacy harnesses (`currentAttemptReplayMetadata ?? replayMetadata`).

**Layer 2 — Classified error routing:**

6. **silentErrorRetryReason** (run.ts): Added `assistantFailoverReason === "server_error"`. Real provider 5xx responses produce `server_error` via the failover classifier — now routed through the retry gate.

## User Impact

Agents recover from transient provider 5xx errors on any turn — even after prior turns executed tools. The retry is blocked only when the **same** attempt had side effects (tools, messaging, cron, spawns), preventing duplicate execution.

**Decision matrix:**
| currentAttemptReplayMetadata | replayMetadata (cumulative) | Retry | Scenario |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------|-------|----------|
| clean | dirty (prior tools) | ✅ YES | #97877 fix |
| dirty (same-attempt tool) | clean | ❌ NO | Prevents duplicate side effects |
| dirty (same-attempt tool) | dirty | ❌ NO | Both agree |
| undefined (legacy harness) | dirty | ❌ NO | Conservative fallback |
| undefined (legacy harness) | clean | ✅ YES | Legacy harness OK |

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: Cumulative `replayMetadata.hadPotentialSideEffects` blocked retry of transient 5xx on later turns. Classified `server_error` was excluded from the retry gate. Same-attempt unsafe tool updates were invisible to the per-attempt metadata signal.

**Real environment tested**: Node 22.19+, local OpenClaw checkout. Three proof levels.

**Proof 1 — Runner-level: `[empty-error-retry]` log capture**

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run.empty-error-retry.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1) / Tests  25 passed (25)
```

Key assertions from the real `runEmbeddedAgent` path (only `runEmbeddedAttempt` mocked):
```
✓ 5xx empty → "[empty-error-retry]" log fires (retry)
✓ prior-turn tools + per-attempt clean → log fires (#97877 fix)
✓ server_error + empty → log fires (classified 5xx retry)
✓ same-attempt tools + per-attempt dirty → log ABSENT (no duplicate side effects)
✓ legacy harness: dirty cumulative + absent per-attempt → log ABSENT (conservative)
```

**Proof 2 — Gateway-level: Live agent recovery with real provider**

Proxy intercepts Turn 2 first attempt (HTTP 200 text/plain → failover: unclassified). Real ZTE Qwen3-235B-A22B API handles all other requests.

```
=== Turn 1: echo hello → side effects accumulated ===
[proxy] chat #1 → real API / chat #2 → real API
hello ← tool output
[agent] run ... stopReason=stop

=== Turn 2: plaintext error → retry → recovery ===
[proxy] chat #3 → text/plain 200 → failover: unclassified
  → shouldRetrySilentErrorAssistantTurn → retry allowed (per-attempt clean)
[proxy] chat #4 → real API (retry)
OK ← recovered reply
[agent] run ... stopReason=stop

Turn 2 used 2 model calls despite HTTP 200 — transport layer does not retry
HTTP 200. The extra call is runner-level empty-error-retry.
```

**Proof 3 — Behavior matrix (5 scenarios)**

```
[1] currentAttempt clean + cumulative dirty (PRIOR TOOLS) → retry YES ✅
[2] currentAttempt dirty + cumulative dirty (SAME-ATTEMPT TOOLS) → retry NO ✅
[3] LEGACY (no currentAttempt), cumulative dirty → retry NO ✅
[4] No metadata at all (5xx before tool subsystem) → retry YES ✅
[5] Both clean (clean session) → retry YES ✅
```

```

node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs (all 7 changed files)

```

**Observed result after fix**: The runner produces `[empty-error-retry]` for both `unclassified` and `server_error` provider failures when the attempt is side-effect-free. Live gateway agent recovers from provider error on Turn 2 after Turn 1's tool execution. Same-attempt tool side effects correctly block retry (via replay state delta). Legacy harnesses without `currentAttemptReplayMetadata` stay conservative via cumulative fallback.

**What was not tested**: Live E2E with a real provider returning HTTP 500 + JSON error body (classified `server_error` path). The `server_error` path is verified through the runner harness with mocked failover classification. Gateway proof covers the `unclassified` path end-to-end with real API.

## Regression Test Plan

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run.empty-error-retry.test.ts --run` — 25 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run.incomplete-turn.test.ts --run` — 114 passed
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on all changed files — exit 0

## Root Cause

Three issues:

1. **Cumulative metadata**: In `attempt.ts`, `replayMetadataFromState(observeReplayMetadata(getReplayState(), observedReplayMetadata))` merges per-attempt data with accumulated session-level state. `rawAttempt.replayMetadata` is always cumulative. The fix computes `currentAttemptReplayMetadata` from the replay state delta (snapshot before tool work vs. current state) merged with `observedReplayMetadata` — giving a genuine per-attempt signal free of prior-turn history.

2. **Missed classified errors**: `silentErrorRetryReason` excluded `server_error`, the failover reason produced by real provider 5xx JSON error responses. The fix adds `server_error` to the retry gate while preserving `shouldRetrySilentErrorAssistantTurn`'s content/tool/side-effect safety checks.

3. **Same-attempt tool tracking gap**: `observedReplayMetadata` was built with `toolMetas: []`, missing replay-unsafe tool updates that `handleToolExecutionEnd` records into `getReplayState()`. The fix captures the replay state delta via `currentAttemptReplayState(initialSnapshot, currentState)` and merges it with `observedReplayMetadata`.

target.title: fix: deliver background task completions through owning sessions
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
Background task completion events can be queued on the real requester session, such as a Telegram topic session, while heartbeat isolation runs the wake in a separate `:heartbeat` session. That can leave the requester without a visible final or blocked completion message even though the background task finished.

Required subagent completions also had a second failure mode: progress-only child output could be presented as a successful handoff instead of being treated as blocked.

## Why This Change Was Made
The fix keeps the behaviour narrow and native:
- Background-task completion wake sources now inspect the owning session queue and bypass heartbeat isolation only for `background-task` and `background-task-blocked` delivery wakes.
- Ordinary heartbeat isolation remains enabled for non-background-task wakes.
- Required subagent completion formatting now reuses the existing required-completion terminal classifier so progress-only output becomes a blocked handoff.
- The required-completion terminal result type now encodes the invariant that blocked completions always carry a status summary.

## User Impact
Users waiting in the original requester session, including Telegram topic sessions, should receive the terminal completion/blocker path instead of losing it to an isolated heartbeat session. Parent agents should no longer treat a progress-only required subagent completion as a successful final deliverable.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(telegram): honor inbound debounce for forwarded bursts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Telegram already supports native inbound debouncing through `messages.inbound`, but forwarded/shared-message bursts used a separate Telegram adapter lane with a hardcoded 80ms delay. When Telegram delivered split chunks more than 80ms apart, OpenClaw could dispatch them as separate turns even when the channel configured a longer native quiet window.

The first PR revision reused the configured inbound window only when it was at least 80ms, so configured positive windows from 1-79ms were still silently floored to the legacy fallback. This update makes every configured positive inbound debounce value apply to the forwarded lane and keeps 80ms only for the disabled `0` path.

## Summary

- make Telegram forwarded/shared-message burst dispatch honour every configured positive native inbound debounce window
- keep the previous 80ms forwarded delay only as the fallback when native inbound batching is disabled
- add regression coverage for both the sub-80ms configured path and disabled fallback path

target.title: fix(macos): read launchd env wrapper auth
target.body:
Closes #98589

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the macOS GUI local gateway auth fallback could miss the launchd-managed gateway token/password when the LaunchAgent uses OpenClaw's generated service-env wrapper file. In that state, the Swift LaunchAgent snapshot only saw inline plist `EnvironmentVariables`, while the Node launchd path had already moved the effective gateway auth values into the wrapper env file.

## Why This Change Was Made

The macOS LaunchAgent snapshot now mirrors the Node launchd plist reader for generated env wrappers: it detects wrapper arguments, reads the generated env file, merges file env over inline plist env, unwraps the effective gateway arguments, and derives local gateway auth from that effective environment. The change is scoped to reading OpenClaw-generated launchd wrapper files and leaves the existing GatewayEndpointStore fallback flow unchanged.

## User Impact

macOS users whose GUI falls back to launchd metadata can still open the local gateway dashboard with the correct auth after the service env values are stored in the generated wrapper file instead of inline in the plist.

target.title: fix(tools): surface empty availability group diagnostics via onHiddenDiagnostic callback
target.body:
## Summary

Empty or malformed plugin tool `availability` groups (e.g. `{ anyOf: [] }`, `{ allOf: ["bad"] }`) silently hid the tool from the plan with no diagnostic. This adds an `onHiddenDiagnostic` callback so `resolvePluginTools` can surface those as authoring warnings, and preserves plugin-authored availability metadata so the planner can evaluate and warn instead of dropping it silently.

Fixes #92361.

## Current diff (warn-only, 6 source files)

- `src/tools/types.ts` — add `onHiddenDiagnostic?` to `BuildToolPlanOptions`.
- `src/tools/planner.ts` — invoke `onHiddenDiagnostic` for each diagnostic that hides a tool.
- `src/tools/availability.ts` — replace the key-presence `hasAvailabilityExpressionShape` with `isValidSignalShape`, which validates `kind` plus the required fields per signal type and rejects non-array `allOf`/`anyOf`.
- `src/plugins/tool-descriptor-cache.ts` — `readAgentToolAvailability` preserves availability-like records so malformed groups still reach the planner/warn path instead of being dropped at capture.
- `src/plugins/tools.ts` — wire `buildToolPlan` + `onHiddenDiagnostic` into `resolvePluginTools`; guard `collectAuthProviderIds`; resolve manifest control-plane enabled plugin ids.
- `src/plugins/manifest-contract-eligibility.ts` — `resolveManifestControlPlaneEnabledPluginIds` helper.

**Not in this diff:** there are no `src/plugin-sdk/*` changes — an earlier SDK-export iteration was dropped. The current behavior is warn-only diagnostics, not a fail-closed/SDK-contract change.

## Crash guard (addresses the P1 review finding)

`collectAuthProviderIds` walks nested `allOf`/`anyOf` entries, which — because `readAgentToolAvailability` intentionally preserves malformed records for the planner to warn on — can be primitives or `null`. It now returns early on non-object/`null` before any `in` check:

```ts
if (!availability || typeof availability !== "object") {
  return;
}
```

so `{ allOf: ["bad"] }` / `{ anyOf: [null] }` no longer throw before diagnostics are emitted. Self-referential availability cycles are handled separately (see **Cycle detection fix** below).

Regression coverage: `resolves tools without throwing when availability holds malformed nested entries` drives `{ allOf: ["bad", null] }` through `resolvePluginTools` with `hasAuthForProvider: () => true` (the exact crash path the review flagged).

## Cycle detection fix (recursion stack — addresses the P2 review finding)

`hasAvailabilityExpressionShape` guards against self-referential plugin-authored
availability. The first iteration kept one cumulative `seen` set for the whole
walk, so a **valid** expression that reuses the same child object across sibling
branches (e.g. `{ allOf: [auth, auth] }`) was wrongly rejected as a cycle:
`isToolAvailabilityExpression` returned `false`, so `tool-descriptor-cache.ts`
dropped the availability and `buildToolPlan` hid the tool.

`seen` is now the **active recursion stack** — each object is added on entry and
removed in a `finally` when its branch resolves. A genuine self-cycle still
short-circuits via `seen.has`, but sibling reuse re-evaluates independently. Sole
consumer is `src/plugins/tool-descriptor-cache.ts:158`
(`if (isToolAvailabilityExpression(availability))`), the exact capture path that
was hiding valid descriptors.

Regression `treats an expression that reuses the same signal object across
siblings as valid shape` asserts `isToolAvailabilityExpression({ allOf: [auth,
auth] })` is `true` (and a real self-cycle is still `false`).

**Negative control** (same regression, run against the pre-fix cumulative-set
version):

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/tools/availability.test.ts -t "reuses the same signal object"

  recursion stack (fixed):        1 passed
  cumulative set (pre-fix):       1 failed  (AssertionError: expected false to be true)
```

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** empty/malformed availability groups were hidden with no diagnostic; malformed nested entries could additionally crash `resolvePluginTools` during auth-provider collection. After this change the planner emits an authoring diagnostic and the collector no longer throws.

**Environment tested:** Node v22.22.0 on Linux, branch `fix/92361-tool-availability-empty-group-warning`, head `16a919be3c`.

**Evidence after fix:**

`isToolAvailabilityExpression` validation:

```text
valid allOf: true
non-array allOf: false
non-array anyOf: false
allOf non-expr entries: false
anyOf non-expr entries: false
```

`resolvePluginTools` with empty `anyOf` (authoring warning surfaced, not silently hidden):

```text
empty group tools=
[plugins] tool descriptor authoring error (proof-plugin/proof_tool): Empty availability anyOf group
```

**Verification on head `16a919be3c`:**

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/tools/planner.test.ts src/plugins/tool-descriptor-cache.test.ts src/plugins/tools.optional.test.ts src/tools/availability.test.ts
  -> 101 passed (availability 11, planner 8, tool-descriptor-cache 12, tools.optional 70)

node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental false
  -> exit 0
```

**What was not tested:** live gateway startup against a real external plugin package shipping malformed availability metadata.

## Compatibility note

This starts preserving plugin-authored `availability` metadata that current `main` and `v2026.6.9` ignore during descriptor capture, surfaced as warn-only diagnostics. Hidden tools behave as before; the only added behavior is the diagnostic warning. Maintainers should explicitly accept the warn-only semantics (or select an overlapping sibling implementation for #92361).

On modern Android, starting a microphone foreground service from the background is restricted, so remote `talk.ptt.start` / `talk.ptt.once` invocations should not start a new capture while the app is backgrounded.

## Why This Change Was Made

This gates new Talk capture starts at the Android runtime boundary. `talk.ptt.once` remains a foreground-only dispatcher command, while `talk.ptt.start` is handled in `NodeRuntime` so idempotent retries for an already-active capture can still return the current capture id. `TalkModeManager.beginPushToTalk(allowNewCapture = false)` owns the final new-capture check to avoid a race between an external active-capture precheck and the actual begin operation.

## User Impact

Background remote commands no longer try to create a new microphone capture path that Android can reject at foreground-service startup time. Existing active PTT sessions can still be stopped/cancelled, and `ptt.start` retries for an active session still reconcile to the same capture id.

## Evidence

- `cd apps/android && ./gradlew :app:testThirdPartyDebugUnitTest --tests ai.openclaw.app.node.InvokeCommandRegistryTest --tests ai.openclaw.app.node.InvokeDispatcherTest --tests ai.openclaw.app.GatewayBootstrapAuthTest --tests ai.openclaw.app.voice.TalkModeManagerTest`

target.title: fix(agents): xAI/Grok requests fail after a stale reasoning replay ("could not decrypt encrypted_content")
target.body:
Closes #97925

_AI-assisted (Claude Code); diagnosed from production gateway logs (see Evidence)._

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users routing reasoning-enabled xAI/Grok (`grok-4.3`) requests through the gateway hit a **full `grok-4.3` outage**: a stale reasoning replay makes xAI return `400 "Could not decrypt the provided encrypted_content…"`, the request fails, and the per-model circuit breaker opens — so **every** subsequent `grok-4.3` call fails with `Circuit breaker open for xai/grok-4.3` until someone intervenes. Any agent or channel on a Grok route is affected.

## Why This Change Was Made

openclaw already recovers from a stale reasoning replay — it strips `encrypted_content` and retries once (`stripResponsesRequestEncryptedContent`). That recovery is gated on `isInvalidEncryptedContentError()`, which only recognized the `invalid_encrypted_content` / `thinking_signature_invalid` codes and messages. xAI/Grok returns a **code-less** prose 400, so the matcher returned `false` and the request failed instead of retrying.

This adds one message match — `encrypted_content` present **and** a decrypt-failure phrase — so the existing strip-and-retry handles xAI too. It is kept deliberately narrow: unrelated "could not decrypt" messages that don't mention `encrypted_content` (e.g. the OAuth-sidecar warning) are excluded, and a negative test asserts that. Blast radius is contained: `isInvalidEncryptedContentError` has a **single caller** (the one-shot retry guard), the retry is **bounded to one attempt**, and it only strips `encrypted_content` — so even a hypothetical over-match costs at most one extra request before the original error surfaces.

## User Impact

xAI/Grok reasoning requests now self-recover from a stale reasoning replay (one transparent retry with `encrypted_content` stripped) instead of failing and tripping the per-model breaker. No more gateway-wide `grok-4.3` outages from this cause, and it survives future xAI model-snapshot rotations. No behavior change for other providers unless they emit the same recoverable error. No UI change.

## Evidence

- **New unit test, red→green.** Mirrors the existing `thinking_signature_invalid` retry test. On clean `main` it fails (no retry); with the fix it passes:
  - `× retries xAI's code-less 'could not decrypt encrypted_content' 400 …` — fails on `main`
  - passes with the fix.
- **Negative test** asserts an unrelated `"could not decrypt"` message (no `encrypted_content`) does **not** retry — proving the match is narrow.
- **oxlint** clean on both files.
- **Validation scope:** ran the affected vitest file (`src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts`) + oxlint locally; relying on CI for the full `pnpm build && pnpm check && pnpm test` lane.
- **Production logs (redacted)** that motivated this — 92 occurrences over ~8h until the session's reasoning state was cleared:
  ```
  [openai-transport] [responses] error provider=xai api=openai-responses model=grok-4.3 status=400 code=undefined message=400 "Could not decrypt the provided encrypted_content. Ensure the value is the unmodified encrypted_content from a previous response."
  res ✗ agent errorMessage=FallbackSummaryError: All models failed (1): xai/grok-4.3: Circuit breaker open for xai/grok-4.3
  ```

target.title: fix(subagents): escalate expected completions on delivery give-up instead of dropping them
target.body:
## What problem this solves On delivery give-up (retry-limit / expiry), an *expected* subagent completion that already produced a result was silently dropped — `clearPendingFinalDelivery` + marked `failed` — so a parent/user that was waiting on it received nothing but a log line. This is the silent-loss path behind a cluster of open reports. The give-up handling in `subagent-registry-lifecycle.ts` has two branches: - **suspend** — preserves the payload (`status: suspended`) so the steering queue can still deliver it to the requester. - **fallback** — clears the payload and marks the run `failed`. The fallback runs whenever the completion is not suspendable (e.g. `cleanup: "delete"`, or a non-`COMPLETE` ended reason) even though the subagent *succeeded and produced a result*. That produced result is then dropped. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[completion ready, delivery to parent fails] --> B{retry/expiry exhausted?} B -- no --> R[retry / defer] B -- "yes (give-up)" --> C{suspendable?
ok outcome + cleanup keep} C -- yes --> S[suspend: payload kept, delivered by steering queue] C -- no --> D{expected completion +
captured result?} D -- "yes (this PR)" --> E[escalate: preserve and surface to user
status suspended, escalated flag] D -- no --> X[clear + failed
nothing to deliver] ``` ## What changed - New shared helper `escalateExpectedCompletionOnGiveUp`: when a completion was expected and a result was captured, preserve it (reusing the suspend path, tagged `escalated`) instead of clearing the payload. - Applied to **both** give-up sites (`finalizeResumedAnnounceGiveUp` and the resume cleanup handler) so neither drops silently. - Adds an `escalated` flag to `SubagentCompletionDeliveryState`. - The retry/expiry decision and the existing suspend path are unchanged. ## Behavior change (delete-mode give-up) This intentionally changes the delete-mode give-up contract: a `cleanup: "delete"` run that produced an *expected* result is now escalated (preserved for delivery) rather than dropped on give-up. Retained completions are bounded by the existing suspended-delivery prune/expiry, so this does not leak runs. The existing test that asserted the drop is updated to assert the new escalation. ## Open question for reviewers The escalation reuses the existing pending-final-delivery path (the steering queue delivers `suspended` entries to `payload.requesterSessionKey`). That stops the silent clear and preserves the result. For the case where the requester chain is fully gone, the entry is bounded by prune/expiry rather than surfaced elsewhere — would you prefer a dedicated root/user escalation notice there, or is preserving-via-the-existing-path the right first step? ## Evidence Local, against the same tree as the branch: - `pnpm tsgo:core`, `tsgo:core:test`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean (exit 0, no type errors) - `oxlint` on the four changed files — 0 warnings / 0 errors - `vitest run src/agents/subagent-registry.test.ts src/agents/subagent-registry-lifecycle.test.ts` — 196 passed, including the new escalate, no-expected-completion, and delete-mode-escalation cases Refs #92433, #67777, #90944, #92116 ### Real behavior proof: retry-limit give-up preserves expected delete-mode completion Redacted local terminal output from PR head `0001cab4d8ed41839a751c6f552670837820e64b`: ```text $ pnpm exec vitest run src/agents/subagent-registry-lifecycle.test.ts src/agents/subagent-registry.test.ts --config test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts -t "escalates" --reporter verbose RUN v4.1.8 /home/koltigin/openclaw-pr-97922 ✓ |agents| src/agents/subagent-registry-lifecycle.test.ts > subagent registry lifecycle hardening > escalates an expected completion with a result on give-up instead of dropping it 27ms ✓ |agents| src/agents/subagent-registry.test.ts > subagent registry seam flow > escalates delete-mode completion runs with a captured result when announce cleanup gives up after retry limit 151ms Test Files 2 passed (2) Tests 2 passed | 98 skipped (100) Duration 4.16s ``` What this proves on the production registry/lifecycle path: - `finalizeResumedAnnounceGiveUp` no longer clears a successful expected completion after retry-limit give-up. - The preserved payload is marked `delivery.status: "suspended"` and `delivery.escalated: true` with `frozenResultText: "final answer"`. - The registry-level retry path keeps the delete-mode run visible through `listSubagentRunsForRequester("agent:main:main")`, so the existing requester steering surface can pick up the suspended payload instead of losing it.

target.title: Fix Codex dynamic tools returning raw payloads
target.body:
Fixes #97913.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's Codex dynamic-tool bridge can receive plugin tool results that are plain payload objects instead of structured `AgentToolResult` envelopes. When a raw payload reaches `convertToolContents(result.content)`, `result.content` is undefined and the bridge can fail with `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'reduce')`.

This PR normalizes raw plugin payloads into `AgentToolResult` envelopes before Codex dynamic-tool middleware/extensions and content conversion, while leaving already-structured `AgentToolResult` responses unchanged.

## Downstream Trigger

The bug was surfaced during evaOS Workbench Mac-control visible-agent proof: direct gateway `tools.invoke` for the same bridge tool succeeded, but the Codex dynamic-tool/model-run path failed before the assistant response. That is downstream evidence only; the defect and fix are in OpenClaw's Codex dynamic-tool runtime boundary.

Workbench release readiness remains tracked downstream in `100yenadmin/evaOS-GUI#480`.

## Summary

- Normalize raw plugin payloads into an `AgentToolResult` before Codex dynamic-tool middleware/extensions and content conversion.
- Keep existing structured `AgentToolResult` responses unchanged.
- Add a regression for a plugin tool whose `execute` returns a plain payload object.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check`
- Direct patched-runtime proof against the installed bundled dynamic-tool bridge: raw payload response normalized to `success: true` and `inputText` JSON.
- Evidence artifact: `/Volumes/LEXAR/Codex/evidence/mac-control-contract-unification/openclaw-tool-repro/after-runtime-normalizer/direct-bridge-raw-payload-proof.json`

## Not Run Locally

- Vitest: this Lexar source worktree has no `node_modules`; `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` reports dependencies missing. GitHub CI owns the full repo test gate.

## Release Boundary

This is OpenClaw runtime/tool-result envelope hardening only. It does not claim evaOS Workbench release readiness or customer readiness.
